query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit excellent properties such as high strength, good ductility, superior corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, making them highly promising for applications in the aerospace, energy, and automotive industries. Among them, the FeNiCrMn HEA demonstrates outstanding corrosion resistance while eliminating the expensive Co element present in the “Cantor” alloy, significantly reducing costs. However, current research on the FeNiCrMn HEA has primarily focused on its corrosion resistance, with relatively limited studies on its mechanical properties. In that context, which method can be used for the stated problem, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using standard uniaxial mechanical testing (tensile/compression tests) on as‐cast FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloys will reveal differences in strength and ductility compared to the canonical Co-containing Cantor alloy, attributable to the removal of Co.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast FeNiCrMn HEA produced by conventional melting methods, having a single solid-solution phase similar to Co-containing HEAs.
generation.intervention: Performing uniaxial tensile and compression tests under controlled temperatures (room temperature and elevated temperature) combined with detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM analysis).
generation.conditions: Room temperature and selected elevated temperatures representative of potential aerospace and automotive applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size, phase homogeneity, and lattice distortion that govern dislocation mobility in the Co-free alloy.
generation.mechanism: Eliminating Co is expected to alter the atomic size mismatch and lattice distortion, which could modify dislocation interactions and thereby affect the balance between yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: FeNiCrMn HEA should retain outstanding corrosion resistance while exhibiting a mechanical property profile (e.g., yield strength and ductility) that differs—potentially with a slight reduction in ductility or modified strengthening due to changed lattice interactions—relative to the well‐studied Co-containing Cantor alloy.
generation.baseline: Mechanical performance data of the traditional CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) alloy.
generation.boundary: Results are limited to as-cast or minimally processed conditions; additional thermomechanical processing may further alter properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude and direction of the strength-ductility shift due solely to Co elimination remain uncertain until measured, due to complex interactions inherent in HEAs.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as-cast FeNiCrMn HEA samples via arc melting. Subject samples to uniaxial tensile and compression tests at room temperature and an elevated temperature (e.g., 600 °C). Perform microstructural analysis using SEM and TEM to correlate grain structure and phase distribution with mechanical performance.
measurements: Microstructural homogeneity (grain size and phase identification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical properties (strength and ductility) of the FeNiCrMn HEA are statistically indistinguishable from those of the canonical Co-containing Cantor alloy and no significant microstructural differences are found, the hypothesis that removing Co significantly alters mechanical behavior will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] .
